items.label: f01-safe-migration-playbook
items.front: eShopOnWeb's safe schema-change playbook: list the steps after editing the entity and its configuration.
items.back: Add the migration naming the context (-c CatalogContext, there are two); read the generated Up/Down and how existing rows are handled; add a default or backfill for non-null columns on populated tables; test on a copy with real-shaped data (not in-memory); have a rollback plan - is Down correct or one-way?

items.label: f04-mediatr-cost
items.front: What does MediatR (CQRS-lite handlers) buy eShopOnWeb, and what does it cost?
items.back: Thin controllers and small, isolated, unit-testable handlers - at the cost of indirection and jump-to-definition friction; overuse adds an indirection tax and fat handlers become the old service in disguise.

items.label: f03-blast-radius
items.front: Rank schema changes by blast radius, and what does a senior ask that a junior skips?
items.back: Adding a nullable column is low risk (additive); making a column non-null, renaming or dropping is high risk. A senior reads the SQL, asks what happens to the existing rows, checks nullability/defaults/locking, plans deploy order (migrate before or after code) and confirms Down works.

items.label: f02-two-contexts
items.front: Why does eShopOnWeb have two DbContexts, and what does that mean for migrations?
items.back: CatalogContext holds domain data and AppIdentityDbContext holds ASP.NET Identity data - a deliberate boundary. Each has its own migrations history, so every dotnet ef command must name the context.

items.prompt: Which DI lifetime mistake does the pattern catalog call the classic composition-root bug?

choices.text: Constructor injection instead of resolving from a service locator
A singleton capturing a scoped DbContext (a captive dependency)
Registering each repository as transient instead of as scoped
Open-generic registration of IRepository<> in a single line

choices: Constructor injection instead of resolving from a service locator
A singleton capturing a scoped DbContext (a captive dependency)
Registering each repository as transient instead of as scoped
Open-generic registration of IRepository<> in a single line

items.explanation: The other options are fine or even recommended; the singleton that outlives the request keeps one DbContext alive across requests and threads.

BasketItem is a value object without an Id, so it cannot be loaded by key
Repositories are registered by hand, and just Basket and Order were registered
BasketItem has no DbSet of its own, so EF is unable to build a repository for it

items.explanation: The constraint stops you loading a BasketItem independently of its Basket - the repository enforces aggregate boundaries.

items.prompt: Why put Guard.Against checks inside CatalogItem rather than only in the controller?

choices.text: Because minimal API endpoints may not throw exceptions
So an invalid CatalogItem cannot exist, whoever constructs it
Because domain guard clauses are checked at compile time
So the UI receives friendlier, localised validation messages

choices: Because minimal API endpoints may not throw exceptions
So an invalid CatalogItem cannot exist, whoever constructs it
Because domain guard clauses are checked at compile time
So the UI receives friendlier, localised validation messages

items.explanation: Guard clauses enforce invariants at the entity boundary; they are distinct from user-facing model validation.

choices.text: EF Core's second-level cache is switched on for the catalog tables in the context
A cached wrapper implements the same interface and DI registers it instead
ASP.NET response-caching middleware wraps the catalog pages in the Web project
CatalogViewModelService inherits from a caching base class added for the purpose

choices: EF Core's second-level cache is switched on for the catalog tables in the context
A cached wrapper implements the same interface and DI registers it instead
ASP.NET response-caching middleware wraps the catalog pages in the Web project
CatalogViewModelService inherits from a caching base class added for the purpose

items.explanation: A cached wrapper implements the same interface and DI registers it in place of the real service. Decorator plus DI: callers never know caching exists; removing it is one DI line. Failure modes include caches with no invalidation.

The NOT NULL change would fail on rows that still hold nulls
It would succeed, and the existing nulls would stay as nulls
The migration's Down method would run automatically instead

items.prompt: OrderItem embeds CatalogItemOrdered (name, picture) as an owned type instead of just a foreign key to the catalog item. Why?

choices.text: EF has no way to map a foreign key from OrderItems to the Catalog table
Owned types are faster to query than a join in SQL Server for large orders
To preserve what was bought even if the catalog item later changes
So past orders can be corrected by editing the catalog item

Owned types are faster to query than a join in SQL Server for large orders
To preserve what was bought even if the catalog item later changes

items.explanation: It is denormalisation for history, mapped as an owned type embedded in OrderItems.

The existing line's quantity grows; only AddItem can change the private item list
A second line is added, and the UI merges duplicate lines when displaying the basket

items.prompt: Checkout calls CreateOrderAsync, then DeleteBasketAsync - each with its own SaveChanges and no explicit transaction. What can a crash between them leave?

choices.text: A deleted basket with no order for it
A half-written order with some items missing
A created order whose basket still lingers
A clean state: EF makes the two saves one transaction

choices: A deleted basket with no order for it
A half-written order with some items missing
A created order whose basket still lingers
A clean state: EF makes the two saves one transaction

items.explanation: Within one SaveChanges EF uses an implicit transaction; across calls there is no atomicity unless you open one, so the consecutive saves are not wrapped together. On the money path that gap is worth calling out.
